Nex Controller and Core API — 0.1.0

Implemented development API for administrator inventory, enrollment, durable operations, appliance adoption and managed-VM creation. Capability-gated storage/network registration, bounded ISO transfer and stopped-VM provisioning use outbound authenticated Core reports. Browser VM consoles use single-use tickets, an outbound host tunnel and a same-origin WebSocket. Central VM power requests (start, shutdown, reboot, force-stop, force-reboot) are durable host operations. Controller-hosted qnetd witness candidate and certificate-registration routes are implemented for Core; two-host SBD arming and witness-loss promotion proof remain withheld.

refresh-inventory

{
  "transport": "POST /api/v1/agent/report response.commands",
  "payload": "None: only operation_id and kind. Created by POST /api/v1/hosts/{id}/operations with a stable request_id; at most one queued or dispatched refresh per host.",
  "result": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/Result"
  },
  "semantics": "Read-only request for a fresh host inventory sample. Core journals it as pending without a managed payload and completes it succeeded when a probe inventory observed after admission is reported, or failed with 'fresh host inventory unavailable before probe deadline'. A pending refresh restarts its deadline after agent restart so it reconciles against a new sample. Delivered without the managed capability. A repeated operation_id is ignored as already admitted, including for legacy journal entries without a stored command; no effects are repeated."
}

pool-member-join

{
  "transport": "POST /api/v1/agent/report response.commands",
  "payload": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/PoolCommand"
  },
  "result": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/Result"
  },
  "semantics": "Reserved master-directed pool command. Core refuses it because membership is admitted only through the authenticated one-use Core-peer exchange; Controller cannot create or replace membership."
}

pool-join

{
  "transport": "POST /api/v1/agent/report response.commands",
  "payload": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/PoolCommand"
  },
  "result": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/Result"
  },
  "semantics": "The one pool command addressed to the joining host rather than the master: its target is pool.member_host_id. Created by POST /api/v1/pools/{id}/members after the master answered the brokered invite. The joining Core runs the whole peer exchange itself, as a durable staged join persisted in its own Core state: precheck, csr, joined, rehomed, advertised, ready. Each stage is individually idempotent, so a crash, reboot or Controller outage resumes at the stage still to perform; the agent re-attempts it from its own loop with no Controller involvement, and reports progress as inventory.managed.join. The invitation and pool CA in the payload are single-use and short-lived; the Controller scrubs them from the stored command as soon as the operation leaves queued and unconditionally 15 minutes after issue. Core refuses the join outright when the host is not enrolled, holds managed VMs or non-local storage, is not the master of its own single-host pool, or is already a member; a host that is admitted but has not finished the remaining stages reports needs_attention and stays a member, never a silent success or a false failure. Ten failed attempts before any membership change end the operation failed rather than retrying an expired invitation forever.",
  "capability": "pool-join-v1 on both the master and the joining Core. The Controller refuses the request rather than degrading to a partial exchange when either side is missing it."
}

pool-storage-reconcile

{
  "transport": "POST /api/v1/agent/report response.commands",
  "payload": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/PoolCommand"
  },
  "result": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/Result"
  },
  "semantics": "Master-directed reconciliation for one NFS or SMB repository. The addressed member pulls the master record over pinned TLS 1.3 peer mTLS, stores an SMB secret only in its own Core credential state, journals native preparation, verifies QEMU access and a cross-Core non-blocking lock, then posts its generation-bound access observation. Before member VM/media work it reserves the current repository generation at the master; failed local work releases that reservation, while a durable definition retains it until the healthy serialized member journal proves it unused. Master source/credential/detach mutations write a Core-owned marker and fail closed while reservations exist. Local ZFS, ordinary iSCSI and generic native disks remain local and are refused/no fencing applies. Controller does not authorize membership, receive SMB secret bytes, or drive retries.",
  "peer_lock": {
    "transport": "POST/DELETE /api/v1/pool/storage/{repository_id}/lock on the Core-peer listener",
    "security": "Pinned TLS 1.3 mTLS; current authenticated pool member. POST checks repository eligibility and generation. Lease ownership is bound to the authenticated member, repository, generation, challenge and mode.",
    "parameters": {
      "generation": "Current repository generation",
      "challenge": "32 hexadecimal characters, generated randomly per attempt",
      "probe_mode": "Optional challenge-byte-v1; absent means legacy byte zero"
    },
    "acknowledgement": "204; challenge-byte-v1 POST echoes X-Nex-Pool-Probe-Mode: challenge-byte-v1. Missing echo selects legacy byte zero; a different nonempty echo fails closed.",
    "semantics": "A nonzero one-byte OFD range derived from the challenge on .nex-peer-lock isolates simultaneous proofs. Only EAGAIN/EACCES establish conflict; after DELETE the member must acquire the same range. A rare range collision fails closed. Unknown modes and malformed challenges are rejected; unavailable generation or lock returns failure. Leases expire after ten seconds and are not VM ownership or fencing authority.",
    "compatibility": "New master supports legacy byte-zero requests. New member falls back to byte zero when an old master omits the acknowledgement, retaining the legacy contention limitation. Core retries periodically with a fresh challenge; no Controller retry job or new durable state.",
    "offset": "SHA-256 of decoded 16-byte challenge; big-endian uint64 of first eight digest bytes, AND ((1<<63)-2), then add one. Byte zero is reserved for legacy peers.",
    "lease_limit": {
      "active": 64,
      "at_capacity": "New leases return lock-unavailable conflict; exact held-lease replay remains idempotent. Release or ten-second expiry frees capacity."
    }
  }
}

The host self-registers /var/lib/libvirt/images as ISO through this same verification, with a host-generated ID, unless any journal entry already holds that path. Succeeded registrations are reported back in Inventory.managed.storage and adopted by a Controller that does not hold them (request_id adopt-storage:<host>:<id>) without redelivery."

storage-zfs-provision

{

  "capability": "storage-zfs-provision-v1",
  "payload": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/ZFSProvisionRequest"
  },
  "result": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/Result"
  },
  "semantics": "Master-directed durable ZFS provisioning. Core owns repository identity, validates stable selected devices immediately before destructive work, journals recovery and performs selected member work through authenticated Core-peer transport. Results are reported in Inventory.managed.zfs_provisions for adoption after Controller replacement."
}

storage-zfs-replace

{
  "transport": "POST /api/v1/agent/report response.commands",
  "capability": "storage-zfs-replace-v1",
  "payload": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/ZFSReplaceRequest"
  },
  "result": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/Result"
  },
  "semantics": "Master-directed replacement of one failed leaf device of a provisioned ZFS pool. It is addressed to the pool master, which accepts it only for its own pool and only for a repository its own record already holds on the named host, and either performs it locally or forwards it to that ready current member over the authenticated Core-peer channel. The executing host revalidates the pool and the disk against a fresh observation, then runs wipefs --all on the replacement and zpool replace; the command is complete when zpool replace returns, and the resilver that follows is reported by the ordinary per-host ZFS observation. ZFS retires the old device itself when the resilver finishes; nothing detaches it. The host journals the operation under its state directory, keyed on operation_id: a redelivered command replays its recorded outcome, a pool already resilvering onto the replacement is adopted as success, an operation ID reused for a different repository, failed leaf or replacement is refused, and an agent interrupted after the wipe resumes from the wipe-started stage, where the wiped disk can no longer match its fingerprint and the identity that survives a wipe (the same by_id, serial and size) is checked instead. The master then records the replacement disk on its own repository record. Master-side refusals are failed results (\"ZFS disk replacement targets another pool\", \"only the pool master may replace a ZFS disk\", \"this pool master has no ZFS repository of that ID on that host\", \"the selected ZFS host is not a ready current member\"); the executing host's refusals arrive as needs_attention carrying its own sentence (\"<device> is no longer part of this pool; check the pool before replacing a disk\", \"<device> is online, so there is nothing to replace\", \"the replacement disk cannot be safely observed\", \"the replacement disk changed since it was selected, or is in use\", \"the replacement disk holds old data and was not confirmed for erasure\", \"the replacement disk could not be cleared\", \"<old> could not be replaced with <new>\")."
}

{
  "transport": "POST /api/v1/agent/report response.commands",

  "payload": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/StorageLifecycleRequest"
  },
  "result": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/Result"
  },
  "semantics": "A name-only update is metadata-only and preserves credentials without reconnecting. Source changes and credential rotation are guarded: rotation requires all referring VMs shut off and no pending or needs_attention disk/media/ISO work. Core compares generation, journals intent before effects, reports needs_attention if rollback is uncertain, and never returns or journals credential bytes."
}

storage-recheck

{
  "transport": "POST /api/v1/agent/report response.commands",
  "capability": "storage-repositories-v1",
  "payload": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/StorageLifecycleRequest"
  },
  "result": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/Result"
  },
  "semantics": "Core observes the registered source without changing configuration or credentials. A missing, replaced, readonly or inaccessible backing source is reported and blocks future disk/media writes; it never uses an empty mountpoint. An identical Controller replay only returns the original operation. Core separately retries at most one due pending/needs_attention storage journal entry per minute in its serialized managed-worker lane, retaining the original result and excluding definitive failures; this continues through Controller loss."
}

network-register

{
  "transport": "POST /api/v1/agent/report response.commands",
  "capability": "managed-vm-v1",
  "payload": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/NetworkRegistration"
  },
  "result": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/Result"
  },
  "semantics": "Verify existing bridge or active libvirt network without edits; for kind vlan, idempotently create bridge <uplink>v<vlan> over the 802.1Q sub-interface, persist it under /etc/network/interfaces.d and refuse uplinks or VLAN devices already used by the host configuration. Refuse, as a failed result, a bridge (shared by kind bridge and vlan) or libvirt network another non-failed registration on this host already holds. The host self-registers <port> untagged for every bridge on a physical NIC or bond through this same verification, with host-generated IDs, unless any journal entry already holds that bridge. Succeeded registrations are reported back in Inventory.managed.networks and adopted by a Controller that does not hold them (request_id adopt-network:<host>:<id>) without redelivery."
}

network-remove

{
  "transport": "POST /api/v1/agent/report response.commands",
  "capability": "pool-resource-removal-v1",
  "payload": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/ResourceLifecycleRequest"
  },
  "result": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/Result"
  },
  "semantics": "Remove a pool VLAN guest network (kind vlan only; anything else is the failed result \"only pool VLAN networks can be removed\"). Core checks the expected generation, then refuses while any VM definition on that host references the network, running or stopped (\"network cannot be removed while used by VM <uuid>\"). On the pool master the agent additionally refuses while any VM in any member's published inventory uses it (\"\u2026 on host <host>\"), and fails closed when membership or that inventory cannot be read or a ready member has not published at the current membership generation (\"pool VM inventory is incomplete; wait for every member to report before removing this network\"). Teardown proves ownership from the /etc/network/interfaces.d/nex-<bridge> stanza Nex itself wrote (\"bridge <b> was not created by Nex; remove it by hand\"), refuses a bridge carrying any port but its own guest port (\"network still has attached interfaces\"), deletes the bridge, deletes <uplink>.<vlan> only when it is a VLAN device with no master that no other Nex stanza names, and removes the stanza. The uplink, the management bridge, host addresses, routes and /etc/network/interfaces are never touched. Teardown is idempotent, so an interrupted removal settles on replay and there is no needs_attention outcome. Success journals a tombstone: the network leaves Inventory.managed.networks as a tombstone row, the host stops rebuilding the bridge, and the Core ID can never be re-registered \u2014 re-adding the same uplink and VLAN mints a new network with a new identity, so VM NICs must be re-pointed."
}

network-update

{
  "transport": "POST /api/v1/agent/report response.commands",
  "capability": "pool-resource-removal-v1",
  "payload": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/ResourceLifecycleRequest"
  },
  "result": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/Result"
  },
  "semantics": "Rename a pool VLAN guest network. The payload carries no uplink, VLAN or source, and the projection copies only the name, so a rename structurally cannot re-plumb a bridge; kind, source, uplink and VLAN are unchanged and the single native effect is one atomic rewrite of the /etc/network/interfaces.d/nex-<bridge> stanza, whose header comment carries the name. The generation becomes expected_generation + 1. A member applies the master's name one generation at a time, so a member several renames behind steps through each one and never reports a generation it did not apply; a member whose journalled source, uplink or VLAN differs reports \"pool network <id> changed uplink or VLAN; remove and re-add it\" instead. A stale expected generation is refused with \"network generation is no longer current; refresh and retry\"."
}

{
  "transport": "POST /api/v1/agent/report response.commands",

With media.url, require iso-download-v1 and zero initial size/hash; Core downloads public HTTP(S) destinations with DNS/redirect address checks, no credentials or environment proxies, capacity limits and ISO validation. media-remove

{
  "transport": "POST /api/v1/agent/report response.commands",
  "capability": "pool-resource-removal-v1",
  "payload": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/ResourceLifecycleRequest"
  },
  "result": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/Result"
  },
  "semantics": "Remove an imported ISO. Core checks the expected generation (\"ISO generation is no longer current; refresh and retry\"), refuses while any VM definition on that host names the ISO as media_id or drivers_media_id, running or stopped (\"ISO cannot be removed while attached to VM <uuid>\"), and on the pool master also refuses for any VM in a member's published inventory (\"\u2026 on host <host>\") and fails closed on incomplete member inventory. Teardown unlinks the published file <storage>/nex-media/<id>.iso and nothing else; a file already gone is success, which is also what the second host on shared storage observes. No VM disk is touched. Success journals a tombstone: the ISO leaves Inventory.managed.media as a tombstone row, and neither VM creation nor a member's shared-media adoption resolves it any more."
}

vm-create

{
  "transport": "POST /api/v1/agent/report response.commands",
  "capability": "managed-vm-v1",
  "payload": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/VMCreateSpec"
  },
  "result": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/Result"
  },
  "semantics": "Create a stopped VM from the full specification: one exclusive new qcow2 per disk inside the VM's own directory on each disk's storage target (sparse when thin, preallocated when not), one interface per NIC with its derived or manual MAC, per-device boot order, the memory mode's balloon and physical-backing configuration, the selected firmware and machine type, and libvirt autostart when requested. Refuse, as a failed result, a name another domain or non-failed journal entry on this host holds, an effective MAC (manual or derived) any domain or journal entry holds, and dedicated memory that, with what is already promised plus the 2 GiB host reserve, exceeds total host memory. When start_after_create is set, start the guest once after the definition is verified and record the outcome in the entry's start field; the creation result is succeeded either way. A retry or reconciliation never starts twice: an interruption at the start step is reconciled by observing libvirt (running means started, otherwise the start outcome reads 'interrupted before the automatic start completed'). A failed start keeps the VM defined and stopped and is reported as a separate outcome <operation-id>:start of kind vm-power, status failed, error 'VM created but not started: <reason>'. Reconcile journal and per-disk ownership on replay. Core resolves storage, network and media references by resource ID, not by pool/host ID, so creation works after re-enrollment under a new Controller. Succeeded definitions are reported back in Inventory.managed.vms and adopted by a Controller that does not hold them (request_id adopt-vm:<host>:<id>) without redelivery."
}

vm-power

{
  "transport": "POST /api/v1/agent/report response.commands",
  "capability": "vm-power-v1",
  "payload": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/VMPowerRequest"
  },
  "result": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/Result"
  },
  "semantics": "Issue one libvirt start/shutdown/reboot/destroy/reset for the named VM on this host. start and force-stop are idempotent against the observed state; shutdown and reboot are ACPI requests the guest may ignore; force-reboot maps to virsh reset, is running-only, and shares reboot's interrupt ambiguity; paused or transitional states are refused. The stage is journaled before the single request so an interruption is reconciled by observation only: succeeded when the observed state proves the outcome, otherwise needs_attention; never a second request. Queue-capable hosts (vm-power-queue-v1) persist FIFO command admission and check after_operation_id is a successful same-VM task before effects; no retry loop for genuine failures. Host-received queued commands survive restart/replacement and are reported as managed outcomes for passive adoption. Shutdown/reboot completion remains ACPI acceptance, not proof of guest shutdown."
}

vm-delete

{
  "transport": "POST /api/v1/agent/report response.commands",
  "capability": "vm-delete-v1",
  "payload": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/VMDeleteRequest"
  },
  "result": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/Result"
  },
  "semantics": "Undefine a stopped managed VM. Requires observed shut off. delete_disks=false retains qcow2 paths in the journal; delete_disks=true unlinks them after undefine. UEFI guests use virsh undefine --nvram. Succeeded deletes omit the VM from Applied.vms and emit DeletedVMs tombstones for Controller mirror removal. An interrupted undefine or wipe resumes when the same operation is delivered again: a domain still defined must be shut off (otherwise needs_attention 'stop the VM so its interrupted delete can finish; observed state is <state>'), undefine repeats with the same flags and a requested wipe repeats over the journaled paths, ignoring files already gone. A later vm-delete for the same VM settles the interrupted one only when delete_disks matches and then fails as already deleted; a different delete_disks choice is refused. Disks of a VM deleted with delete_disks=true no longer count as storage-detach dependencies."
}

vm-media

{
  "transport": "POST /api/v1/agent/report response.commands",
  "capability": "vm-media-v1",
  "payload": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/VMMediaRequest"
  },
  "result": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/Result"
  },
  "semantics": "Insert a verified ISO into, or eject media from, the named VM's CD drive on this host with one libvirt change-media (live and persistent). Insert attaches an empty CD drive first when the domain has none; eject on a drive that is already empty (checked against the live definition of a running VM) succeeds without any libvirt call and never attaches a drive. The resolved media path and the changing-media stage are journaled in one write immediately before the change, so an interruption before that write is simply re-applied and one after it is reconciled by observing the domain: succeeded when the drive holds the requested media (or none, for eject), otherwise needs_attention. Core records only media_id in the VM's journaled specification; boot order values are never rewritten because change-media leaves every device's bootindex as it is."
}

vm-update

{
  "transport": "POST /api/v1/agent/report response.commands",
  "capability": "vm-update-v1",
  "payload": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/VMCreateSpec"
  },
  "result": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/Result"
  },
  "semantics": "Apply one revision of an existing VM's definition; refuse a revision other than current + 1. Classify the difference from the journal's current definition (NeedsStop): a shut-off guest is redefined after any new disks are allocated and a rename (domrename), with the same capacity, name and MAC conflict checks as creation; a running guest takes only device additions, removals and media changes, applied with attach-device/detach-device --persistent and change-media --live --config, and is refused before any effect for anything else; an added interface whose MAC is still live after an earlier removal the guest has not released is refused and the task fails before any effect. Disks are matched by name and keep their journaled target names; interfaces by MAC. Removed disk files are retained and listed in the journal. The persistent definition and per-disk ownership are then observed against the regenerated XML by device identity; an interruption is reconciled by observation, except a UEFI-to-BIOS change interrupted after its undefine (stage cleaning-nvram or defining), which Core finishes by confirming the domain is absent and defining the journaled BIOS XML, and which refuses to undefine a UEFI domain that reappeared. A stopped edit that renames the VM and changes Secure Boot runs the read-only Secure Boot checks first, then domrename, then the variable-store edit and define. The journal reports the highest succeeded revision as the VM's current definition."
}

pool-maintenance

{
  "transport": "POST /api/v1/agent/report response.commands",
  "payload": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/PoolCommand"
  },
  "result": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/Result"
  },
  "semantics": "Addressed to the pool master, never to the host being drained: the master owns the membership record the flag lives in, and entering or leaving maintenance never contacts the drained host. Only membership.master_host_id, member_host_id, enabled and the optional expected_version are on the wire. The master sets PoolMember.Maintenance and MaintenanceSince in its own pool-peer.json and deliberately does not bump the membership generation, so draining a host cannot invalidate an in-flight placement, a published inventory or a peer generation check. enabled is a desired state, so re-sending it succeeds and leaves maintenance_since unmoved, which is what makes an exact retry after a lost reply safe. Core refusals are definite failed results: \"only the pool master records maintenance mode\", \"no such member of this pool\", \"an ejected host has no maintenance state\", \"pool membership is unavailable\", \"pool membership changed since this request was composed; review the pool and try again\", \"maintenance command carries no maintenance request\" and the PoolCommand.Valid() texts. A durable save that may not have landed is reported needs_attention with \"maintenance mode could not be recorded durably\"; the next inventory report states the truth and the exact retry is safe. While the flag is set the master refuses new placement, define and start admission for that host with \"the selected VM host is in maintenance mode; take it out of maintenance before placing or starting VMs on it\", and skips it in autostart-by-placement. It never blocks stop, shutdown or force-stop, never stops a running guest, never blocks local recovery and never blocks the member's own convergence.",
  "capability": "pool-maintenance-v1 on the pool master. The Controller offers no maintenance control without it."
}

management-network

{
  "transport": "POST /api/v1/agent/report response.commands",
  "payload": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/ManagementNetworkRequest"
  },
  "result": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/Result"
  },
  "semantics": "Addressed to the host whose management network is being changed, and performed entirely by it. Two identities ride in the request: operation_id is the command envelope's own, unique per command, because it is the managed journal's replay key; change_id names the change Core acts on, which is the operation_id the host recorded when it staged it and reports back in inventory.management_network. stage validates and renders the spec, snapshots /etc/network/interfaces, /etc/dhcpcd.conf and /etc/resolv.conf and writes <state-dir>/management-network.json, touching nothing in /etc. apply records the applied stage and its deadline before any file is written, then renames the three rendered files into place and bounces br0; a failed write or a bridge that will not come up rolls back immediately. confirm keeps the change, clears the deadline, bumps the revision and drops the snapshot. cancel discards a staged change or rolls back an applied, unconfirmed change at the operator's request. The host rolls back by itself when the deadline passes and when it finds it rebooted after the apply, at agent start, on every probe tick and from an exact in-process timer; no Controller is involved. Core refusals are definite failed results. Conflicts end with \"management network conflict\": \"a management network change is already applied and waiting to be confirmed or rolled back\", \"management network revision is <n>, not <m>\", \"no management network change is staged as <id>\", \"no management network change is applied as <id>\", \"management network change <id> is <stage>\", \"management network change <id> is <stage> and cannot be cancelled\", \"the rollback deadline for <id> has passed; the previous configuration is being restored\", \"this host has not yet been reached over an address of br0 itself under the new configuration; a Controller report that arrived over another interface, or a local API call from this machine, does not count\", \"the host network configuration changed since this edit was staged; stage it again\". Plain failures are \"management network command carries no request\", \"management network request does not match its command\", \"the confirmation does not name this host\", \"this host cannot read its own name to check the confirmation\", the ManagementNetworkRequest.Valid() and spec validation texts, \"rollback window must be between 2m0s and 30m0s\", \"<path> is not a regular file (<mode>); replace it with a plain file before changing the management network\", \"<path> is missing; Nex Core will not create a management network configuration it cannot prove it rendered\" and \"<path> was not written by Nex Core or the Nex installer; edit it from the host console instead\". Guest VLAN bridges under /etc/network/interfaces.d are never read, written or brought down, and /etc/systemd/network/*.link is never rewritten, so interface renames are not part of a staged change. Re-staging the same change id with a different spec is refused with \"management network change <id> is already staged with a different configuration\": an exact retry replays the staged change, while the same id carrying another configuration is not a retry at all, and answering \"succeeded\" would report on the recorded change while the operator is looking at the one they just sent.",
  "capability": "management-network-v1 on the target host. The Controller offers no management network control without it."
}

pool-transfer

{
  "transport": "POST /api/v1/agent/report response.commands",
  "payload": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/PoolCommand"
  },
  "result": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/Result"
  },
  "semantics": "Addressed to the pool's current master, never to the subject host: the master owns the authority being moved, and it drives every step itself. action is master-change, eject or transfer-cancel; only membership.master_host_id, member_host_id, the action and the optional expected_version are on the wire. The master records a durable Transfer record in its own pool-peer.json before anything else happens and advances it on every tick, so the operation survives a Controller that is restarted, replaced or disconnected, and a power cycle of either host. Terminal results: succeeded; failed, which is a decision and means nothing moved; and needs_attention, which is not an error but \"durable and still running \u2014 the hosts finish it\". Core refusals include \"only the pool master starts a master change or an eject\", \"no such member of this pool\", \"only a ready member with a peer endpoint can become the pool master\", \"another pool authority transfer is already in progress on this pool\", \"pool authority is frozen for a master change; retry when it completes\", \"pool authority was handed to another host; this host is no longer the pool master\", \"host <id> still owns pool VM records (<ids>); move or delete them before ejecting it\", \"host <id> still holds a pool-shared storage reservation on <repo>; let it finish before ejecting it\", \"no pool authority transfer is in progress on this pool\", \"the pool authority transfer in progress has another target\" and \"the target has already activated this pool authority; the master change can only go forward\", \"host <id> is already removed from this pool's membership; the eject can only go forward\" and \"this pool promotion has powered the old pool master off; it cannot be cancelled and can only go forward\". A cancelled eject records \"the pool member eject was cancelled by an operator\"; a cancelled master change records \"the pool master change was cancelled by an operator\". A cancel is accepted only before the transfer's first irreversible durable step, and Core reports that answer itself as PoolTransferStatus.cancellable rather than leaving a caller to judge by stage name: a master change stays cancellable through freeze, replicate and activate, including the hand-off window, where it succeeds only if the target proves under its own lock that it never activated; an eject stays cancellable through freeze and remove, and is refused once the membership without that member has been written; a promotion is never cancellable, because it has powered a host off. The reported flag is computed from the same predicate the cancel is gated on, so the two cannot drift. While the transfer holds the freeze every pool authority write on the master is refused rather than queued; running guests keep running, stop is never refused and storage reservation releases are never frozen. Before a planned master change or eject records its first freeze, Core refuses unresolved backup journal work, pending backup runs and pending metadata receipts with \"backup operation is unresolved; finish or reconcile it before changing pool authority\"; the check and first durable freeze hold the same backup authority lock. Fenced promotion may inherit pending backup authority and reports those runs/receipts needs_attention, retaining restore pins instead of queuing their native work on the new master.",
  "capability": "pool-authority-transfer-v1 on the pool master, on the selected host and on every ready member. The Controller offers no master change or eject without it on the master, because a member that cannot re-point would keep following a host that is no longer the pool master."
}

pool-promote

{
  "summary": "Promote a surviving member to pool master after fencing the old one",
  "target": "The promotion candidate itself \u2014 the one pool command besides pool-join that is not addressed to the master, because the master is the host that is gone.",
  "payload": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/PoolCommand"
  },
  "capability": "pool-authority-transfer-v1 on the promotion candidate. S6 adds no new capability string.",
  "semantics": "One durable, resumable machine keyed by operation_id, driven entirely on the candidate. Payload: PoolCommand{request_id, action: promote, member_host_id (the candidate), fence_confirmed: true, fence_host_ids}. fence_host_ids is the exact set of hosts the operator agreed to power off, as the verdict's fence_host_ids named them \u2014 the old pool master, and every other host that blocks the promotion and can be excluded by a fence. Core refuses without it (\"this promotion will power off other hosts; confirm the hosts this pool reports before it can run\") and compares it again at run time against the set it computes itself, so a pool that changed since the preflight stops the promotion rather than quietly fencing something new: \"this promotion must power off <ids>, which is not what was confirmed; confirm the hosts this pool reports and try again\" and \"this promotion no longer needs to power off any host; review the pool and try again\". A host is never powered off without having been named to the operator first. No membership travels: the candidate reads the signed replica it already holds. It moves nothing until Core has proved replica integrity, replica supremacy, accepted ownership and a fence proof Core itself produced \u2014 an independently observed power-off of the recorded fence target, digest-bound to this pool, this excluded host, this operation and this generation, and at most 15 minutes old. A returned fence agent status, a timeout, a missed heartbeat or an operator assurance cannot construct one. The whole verdict is re-proved immediately before activation, so a member that returned between the fence and the activation stops it; activation adopts VM ownership first, then makes this host master at generation + 1 in one atomic write, and an interrupted promotion resumes at the stage that did not complete. Terminal results: succeeded; failed, which is a decision and means nothing moved; and needs_attention, which is not an error but \"durable and still running\". Core's own refusals arrive on the operation and are surfaced verbatim in last_promotion: \"the pool master <id> is reachable and holds this pool's authority; change the pool master with a planned master change instead of promoting\", \"the pool master <id> has no recorded fence profile; record one before promoting\", \"the pool master <id> has not been fenced for this promotion; Core fences it and observes the power-off when the promotion is confirmed\", \"this promotion has no fence proof for the old pool master\", \"this fence proof excludes another host\", \"this fence proof belongs to another promotion\", \"this fence proof is not bound to this promotion\", \"this fence proof is older than 15m0s; fence the old pool master again\", \"the old pool master was not excluded: <native reason>\", \"pool host <ids> holds a newer pool authority than this host; promote it instead\", \"pool VM <ids> is recorded differently by the host that owns it; resolve that before promoting\", \"this host holds no pool authority replica; it cannot be promoted\", \"this host's pool authority replica was never verified\", \"this host holds no fence credential for <host>; it cannot fence it, so it cannot be promoted over it\", \"the replicated fence credential is not addressed to this host\", \"the replicated fence credential is unreadable\", \"this host already holds different material under that fence credential reference\", \"this host is already the master of its pool\", \"promoting this host powers the old pool master off; confirm that before the promotion can run\" and \"a pool promotion is performed by the candidate itself\". A cancel is never accepted: \"this pool promotion has powered the old pool master off; it cannot be cancelled and can only go forward\". This command is the manual promotion path. A separate Core-owned automatic path is limited to eligible two-host pools with Host fencing enabled and a recorded usable BMC profile; no automatic watchdog, storage lease or Nex Witness path exists. There is no election; no force, override, \"declare host lost\" or timeout-based path exists or may be added."
}

pool-fence-profile

{
  "summary": "Record or clear how a member of this pool would be power-fenced",
  "target": "The pool master, which owns the durable membership record the profile lives in.",
  "payload": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/PoolCommand"
  },
  "capability": "pool-authority-transfer-v1 on the pool master.",
  "semantics": "Payload: PoolCommand{request_id, action: fence-profile, membership.master_host_id, member_host_id, fence}. A null fence clears the profile. The profile is written into the master's durable membership and replicated with it, so a promoted master inherits it and a fresh Controller re-adopts it from the master's reported inventory. No credential material travels on this command: credential_ref names a file the existing one-time encrypted fence-credential handoff has already delivered to the master, and Core refuses to record a profile whose material it does not hold \u2014 \"this host holds no fence credential for <host>; deliver it to this host before recording the profile\" and \"this host's fence credential material for <host> is larger than this pool replicates; shorten it before recording the profile\". Core also refuses at record time any profile it could not verify, in the shape \"this fence profile cannot be verified by this host: <reason>\", releasing the delivered credential when it does: \"this host does not report a unique hardware identity, so a management controller cannot be confirmed to be its own\", \"this management controller did not answer, so the machine behind it could not be identified\", \"this management controller rejected the recorded account, so the machine behind it could not be identified\", \"the management controller at this address reports a different machine than the host it is recorded for; nothing was powered off\", \"a management controller fence device needs the account Nex Core signs in with\", \"virsh fencing needs an immutable domain UUID target\" and \"SCSI persistent-reservation fencing is unsupported\". Before any power-off Nex Core asks the management controller which machine it manages \u2014 IPMI Get System GUID, in either documented byte order, or the Redfish ComputerSystem.UUID \u2014 and compares it with the target host's own SMBIOS system UUID in the master's membership record. A mismatch, a missing recorded UUID and an unreadable controller each refuse the fence and power nothing off. Other refusals: \"only the pool master records a fence profile\", \"no such member of this pool\", \"an ejected host has no fence profile\". Recording a usable profile for the master itself is what opts a pool into fence-verified promotion, and therefore into the boot rule of a restarted master; clearing it is durable and is only released once every ready member has acknowledged a replica built without it."
}

pool-bmc-provisioning

{
  "summary": "Let a host configure its own management controller for fencing again",
  "target": "The pool master, which owns the durable membership record this decision lives in.",
  "payload": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/PoolCommand"
  },
  "capability": "pool-authority-transfer-v1 on the pool master.",
  "semantics": "Payload: PoolCommand{request_id, action: bmc-provisioning, membership.master_host_id, member_host_id}. It says one thing \u2014 this host may configure its own management controller again \u2014 and re-sending it is a success, because it is a desired state and not a transition. The master clears PoolMember.bmc_provisioning_disabled and the host's last management-controller report, and the host creates the account on its own next pass. The opposite direction is not a command: clearing a Core-provisioned fence profile sets the flag, removes the account and stops provisioning, in the one path that clears a profile. Refusals: \"this command carries no management controller request\", \"only the pool master records whether a host configures its own management controller\", \"pool membership is unavailable\", \"no such member of this pool\", and the authority-write refusals a fence profile takes while a master change is in flight."
}

pool-host-fencing

{
  "summary": "Turn this pool's host fencing on or off",
  "target": "The pool master, which owns the durable membership record this setting lives in.",
  "payload": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/PoolCommand"
  },
  "capability": "pool-host-fencing-v1 on the pool master.",
  "semantics": "Payload: PoolCommand{request_id, action: host-fencing, membership.master_host_id, enabled}. It names no member, because the setting is the pool's. The master records PoolMembership.host_fencing_disabled as the negative of enabled and replicates it with the pool's records; every host reads it from the copy it already holds. It is a desired state and not a transition, so re-sending the state already recorded answers succeeded. Turning it on arms nothing by itself: Nex Core arms a host's watchdog only where every prerequisite in PoolFenceSummary.prerequisites holds, and the quorum line is unknown until this pool runs a quorum service. Refusals: \"this command carries no host fencing request\", \"only the pool master records whether host fencing is on\", \"pool membership is unavailable\", and the authority-write refusals a fence profile takes while a master change is in flight."
}

host-system-disk-replace

{
  "transport": "POST /api/v1/agent/report response.commands",
  "payload": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/SystemDiskReplaceRequest"
  },
  "result": {
    "$ref": "#/components/schemas/Result"
  },
  "semantics": "Addressed to the host whose mirror is rebuilt and performed entirely by it; nothing is pool-scoped and nothing is kept by the Controller. The durable record is the md superblocks and the installer's /etc/mdadm/mdadm.conf, whose array UUID does not change when a member is added. Core journals the operation under its state directory, keyed on operation_id: a redelivered command replays its recorded outcome, an array that already has the replacement as a member is adopted without wiping it again, and an agent interrupted after the wipe resumes from the wipe-started stage, where the wiped disk can no longer match its fingerprint and the identity that survives a wipe (the same by_id, serial and size) is checked instead. A member whose disk the kernel no longer exposes is the failure being repaired and is passed over. Refusals are definite failed results carrying Core's own sentence: \"/dev/mdN is not degraded, so there is no member to replace\", \"<device> is a <level> array; only a RAID1 mirror is rebuilt this way\", \"<device> has no working member to copy from; restore this host instead\", \"the replacement disk changed since it was selected, or is in use\", \"the replacement disk holds old data and was not confirmed for erasure\", \"Nex Core cannot read this host's RAID arrays\", \"this host has no array <mdN>\", \"<disk> already holds a working member of <array>\", \"the replacement disk cannot be safely observed\", \"the replacement disk is smaller than the remaining system disk\".",
  "capability": "host-system-disk-replace-v1"
}

The local Core API accepts one stable snapshot operation ID, optional mode (omitted/stopped for shut-off guests; crash or quiesced for a running guest), and exact current VM definition, persists intent, obtains the current pool-master reservation, captures native disk and firmware recovery state, and settles the compact descriptor in the master catalog before reporting success. POST /api/v1/session

Sign in as administrator

Validates existing administrator credentials and browser origin. Sets __Host-nex_session with Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict, Path=/ and no Domain. Each login creates a new session; at most 64 active sessions per service. Sessions expire after 30 minutes without an authenticated mutation and eight hours absolutely; GET/HEAD polling does not renew them. Legacy unprefixed cookies are not accepted; sign in again after upgrade. Existing password hashes remain valid; new administrator bootstrap passwords must be nonempty valid UTF-8, at most 1024 UTF-8 bytes, without CR, LF or NUL; there is no minimum length or complexity rule. Login admission permits at most five valid-length attempts per one-minute actual peer-IP window, two concurrent password checks per service, and 4096 tracked peers. Forwarded client-IP headers are ignored. Login returns 429 when rate/concurrency/table or 64-session capacity is exhausted; bounded retries must not create an unbounded loop.

GET /api/v1/pools

List pools

Implemented in development product 0.1.0, protocol v1. Read-only; safe to retry. Pools are never created by administrators: each enrolling Core host becomes the master of a new pool named after its hostname (master_host_id). Membership itself is owned by the pool master: this list and POST /api/v1/pools/{id}/members relay and display it, and the Controller never authorizes or persists membership intent of its own. The Core local API keeps the same authenticated member join flow as a host-local recovery path. Master change and member eject remain unavailable. Results represent persisted controller state.

GET /api/v1/pools/{id}/members

Show the pool master's reported membership and convergence

Administrator session. Read-only projection of what the pool master reports: its inventory.managed.membership, each member's connection freshness, its four convergence checks (pool-storage-reconciliation, pool-network-reconciliation, pool-media-reconciliation, pool-authority-replica) and counts of the master's member_access rows that are healthy, pending, failed or stale. It stores nothing and computes no membership of its own. authoritative is true only while the master's connection is fresh; when it is not, status, error, checks, access counts, failures, maintenance and maintenance_since are reported as unknown, null or empty rather than presenting the last mirror as current, and the client must show them as unknown. peer_origin is part of the master's durable record rather than an observation of it and is reported either way. Each member also carries its own reported staged join, its own reported guest list (known false when that host is not fresh), the newest pool-maintenance operation this Controller holds for it, and the authority replica as the member and the master each report it. Implemented in development product 0.1.0.

POST /api/v1/pools/{id}/members

Add an enrolled host to this pool

Administrator session, same HTTPS Origin and X-CSRF-Token required. The Controller makes exactly two calls and drives nothing: it asks the pool master for a single-use join invitation over one report round trip (pool_requests/pool_results, 45-second deadline), then hands that invitation to the joining host as one durable pool-join command. The joining Core performs the whole peer exchange with the master itself and reports progress as inventory.managed.join; a Controller that is lost after the command changes nothing about the outcome. Both hosts must advertise pool-join-v1. The Controller validates only what it can see (pool and host exist, both fresh and not revoked, the joining host is the master of its own single-host pool with no managed VMs and no non-local storage, peer_origin is a bare https origin); every refusal that matters is still the master's and is relayed verbatim. master_url is an optional override that the web UI never sends: the master's own reported peer_origin wins when it has one; otherwise Core records the supplied master_url, or when none is supplied the origin it works out itself (https://<its default-route source address>:9444), as the master's own peer_origin the first time it issues an invitation. The joining host is handed the master_url from the invitation. Persist request_id before sending: an identical retry returns the original operation with 200 and never starts a second join, while the same request_id with any changed field (master_url included) conflicts. The invitation and pool CA are never returned, listed, logged or audited; the stored command is scrubbed of them as soon as the operation leaves queued and unconditionally 15 minutes after issue. Joining is not one-way: a member can be ejected with DELETE /api/v1/pools/{id}/members/{host_id}, the pool master can be changed with POST /api/v1/pools/{id}/master, and a surviving member can be promoted with POST /api/v1/pools/{id}/master/promote when the master is lost. Implemented in development product 0.1.0.

          }
        }
      }
    },
    "499": {
      "description": "The client disconnected while the handler was waiting for the pool master's answer (\"the client disconnected before the pool master answered; retry with the same request_id\"). Nothing was written and the broker entry was released; no client reads this status, and the same request_id is safe to retry.",
      "content": {
        "application/json": {
          "schema": {
            "$ref": "#/components/schemas/Error"
          }
        }
      }
    },
    "500": {
      "description": "Controller storage or lookup failure (\"storage unavailable\", \"inventory unavailable\", \"pool join storage failed\", \"operation lookup failed\", \"resource lookup failed\"). Retry with the same request_id.",
      "content": {
        "application/json": {
          "schema": {
            "$ref": "#/components/schemas/Error"
          }
        }
      }
    },
    "504": {
      "description": "The master did not answer the brokered invite request within 45 seconds. The body is a PoolResult, not the usual error object, and carries \"the pool master did not return a join invitation before the deadline; retry with the same request_id\". No command was created and no membership changed; retrying with the same request_id is safe.",
      "content": {
        "application/json": {
          "schema": {
            "$ref": "#/components/schemas/PoolResult"
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

POST /api/v1/pools/{id}/members/{host_id}/maintenance

Drain a pool member, or take it out of maintenance

Administrator session, same HTTPS Origin and X-CSRF-Token required. Relays one durable pool-maintenance command to the pool master, which owns the flag inside the membership record it already keeps; the Controller records no drain of its own and the command is never sent to the host being drained. Maintenance refuses new VM placement, definition and start admission on that host and skips it in autostart; it stops no running guest and never blocks stop, shutdown or force-stop, so there is nothing to confirm and no confirmation field. The refusals below are only what the Controller can already see from host reports: the master is fresh, active and advertises pool-maintenance-v1, it has reported a membership, the host is a non-ejected member of it, and expected_version matches what it last reported. Core checks every one of them again against its own record, and its refusals arrive as a failed operation with conflict marked in GET /api/v1/pools/{id}/members, not as an HTTP status here. Implemented in development product 0.1.0.

GET /api/v1/pools/{id}/join-candidates

Preview which hosts could join this pool

Administrator session. Read-only presentation of host-reported facts for the "Add host to pool" dialog: enrolled, non-revoked hosts in the same site that are not already in this pool, each with a compatibility preview composed from both hosts' own reported inventory (connection, agent version, capability lists, existing membership, managed VMs, non-local storage, NIC names against each pool VLAN's uplink, CPU baseline). Each row is compatible, will_not_converge or refuses_join; eligible is false if and only if some row is refuses_join, and will_not_converge rows do not block a join. This is a preview, not an authorization: every refusal is decided again by Core when the join is submitted, and a candidate listed as eligible can still be refused. Implemented in development product 0.1.0.

POST /api/v1/enrollment-tokens

Issue a site-bound enrollment token

Implemented in development product 0.1.0, protocol v1. Creates a short-lived single-use secret bound to a site; the enrolling host becomes the master of a new pool in that site. POST /api/v1/hosts/probe

Probe a host's local API TLS certificate

Implemented in development product 0.1.0, protocol v1. Performs an insecure TLS 1.3 handshake to the given address (default port 9443) purely to capture the leaf certificate nex-core-local presents; it establishes no trust and stores nothing. POST /api/v1/sites/{id}/hosts

Add a host by address and root password

Implemented in development product 0.1.0, protocol v1. Replaces manual token enrollment for a reachable host: the operator first confirms the certificate fingerprint returned by probeHost, then submits it here alongside the host's root password. The Controller re-verifies that same fingerprint with a constant-time comparison during its own outbound TLS handshake to the host — a mismatch fails the handshake and returns 502 before the password is ever sent. On a verified connection the Controller signs in to the host's local API (POST /api/local/v1/session), mints a fresh site-bound enrollment token (the same token contract createEnrollmentToken uses), and pushes it to the host's local enrollment endpoint together with the Controller's own served HTTPS certificate (the -tls-cert file, not the host-identity CA) as the trust the host pins for its Controller connection; the host then enrolls with this Controller through the existing agent-enrollment contract and becomes the master of a new pool in this site. The root password is used once for that single sign-in and is never stored, logged, or echoed back, including in error messages. Unknown site_id returns 400. Optional host_id re-enrolls a revoked host whose pool belongs to this site (409 otherwise, checked before any network attempt). A wrong password returns 401; a login rate limit returns 429 with the host's own message. If the host reports it is already enrolled under a different identity, this returns 409 with that host_id — retrying the same add-host call after a lost response is safe and resolves the same way: fetch inventory to see the enrolled host. Any other host-side failure returns 502 naming the controller_url the host was asked to reach, and any token minted for the attempt is deleted. If the Controller process has no served certificate configured, 503 is returned before any host contact; use manual enrollment. One host-side enrollment refusal is a normal wait rather than a failure and is answered as such: a host that relays this Controller's own "pool identity is held; the pool master has not reported this ready member" gets 409 with retryable true and the host's own words preserved in host_error, not the 502 every other host-side failure keeps. It happens while a pool member is added to a replacement Controller before its pool master has reported it; connect the master first, or retry once it has reported the member.

Complete operation contract (parameters, authentication, responses) 
{
  "operationId": "addSiteHost",
  "summary": "Add a host by address and root password",
  "description": "Implemented in development product 0.1.0, protocol v1. Replaces manual token enrollment for a reachable host: the operator first confirms the certificate fingerprint returned by probeHost, then submits it here alongside the host's root password. The Controller re-verifies that same fingerprint with a constant-time comparison during its own outbound TLS handshake to the host \u2014 a mismatch fails the handshake and returns 502 before the password is ever sent. On a verified connection the Controller signs in to the host's local API (POST /api/local/v1/session), mints a fresh site-bound enrollment token (the same token contract createEnrollmentToken uses), and pushes it to the host's local enrollment endpoint together with the Controller's own served HTTPS certificate (the -tls-cert file, not the host-identity CA) as the trust the host pins for its Controller connection; the host then enrolls with this Controller through the existing agent-enrollment contract and becomes the master of a new pool in this site. The root password is used once for that single sign-in and is never stored, logged, or echoed back, including in error messages. Unknown site_id returns 400. Optional host_id re-enrolls a revoked host whose pool belongs to this site (409 otherwise, checked before any network attempt). A wrong password returns 401; a login rate limit returns 429 with the host's own message. If the host reports it is already enrolled under a different identity, this returns 409 with that host_id \u2014 retrying the same add-host call after a lost response is safe and resolves the same way: fetch inventory to see the enrolled host. Any other host-side failure returns 502 naming the controller_url the host was asked to reach, and any token minted for the attempt is deleted. If the Controller process has no served certificate configured, 503 is returned before any host contact; use manual enrollment. One host-side enrollment refusal is a normal wait rather than a failure and is answered as such: a host that relays this Controller's own \"pool identity is held; the pool master has not reported this ready member\" gets 409 with retryable true and the host's own words preserved in host_error, not the 502 every other host-side failure keeps. It happens while a pool member is added to a replacement Controller before its pool master has reported it; connect the master first, or retry once it has reported the member.",

GET /api/v1/hosts/{id}/network

Read a host's management network and any change in flight

Administrator session required. Every field is a host report or this Controller's own operation history: the host's durable record (stage, spec, rollback deadline and time remaining), its reported interface inventory, its management-network health check and the newest management-network operation. The Controller stores none of it, so a replacement Controller returns the same answer as soon as the host reports. While the host is not fresh, state is "unknown" and check is null, but the record itself is still returned so a running rollback deadline stays visible instead of reading as success or failure. Implemented in development product 0.1.0.

POST /api/v1/hosts/{id}/network

Stage, apply, confirm or cancel a host's management network change

Administrator session, same HTTPS Origin and X-CSRF-Token required. Relays one durable management-network command per step to the host, which renders, applies, times and rolls back its own configuration; the Controller computes nothing and keeps no copy of the change. stage writes nothing into /etc. apply swaps the three rendered files and bounces the management bridge, and starts the host's own rollback timer: unless a confirm arrives before the deadline, or if the host reboots first, the host restores the previous configuration by itself, with no Controller involved. confirm keeps the new configuration and is refused by Core until the host has observed its own connectivity over it. cancel discards a staged change, or immediately rolls back an applied, unconfirmed change. The refusals below are only what the Controller can already see from this host's reports; Core checks every one of them again, including the confirmation, which it alone can bind to itself, and its own refusals arrive as a failed operation rather than as an HTTP status here. Implemented in development product 0.1.0.

POST /api/v1/agent/enroll

Enroll a Core host

Implemented in development product 0.1.0, protocol v1. Outbound HTTPS; agent must verify Controller identity before transmitting its site-bound token. Provide a signed PEM ECDSA P-256 CSR and nonblank hostname (maximum 200 UTF-8 bytes, no CR/LF/NUL). Identity is host-owned: the host presents the host_id it generated and, as its pool's master, the pool_id and pool_name it keeps, and the Controller adopts them unchanged, so a replacement Controller recovers the pool with its original ID and name. host_id and pool_id must be canonical lowercase UUIDs (or the 64-hex form issued to hosts enrolled before host-owned identity) and pool_name a valid name, else 400. A fresh enrollment creates the pool in the token site with this host as its master, then records the host in that pool in the same transaction (audit pool.create and host.enroll); older agents that present no identity get Controller-minted IDs and a pool named after the hostname, which the response reports for the host to keep. A presented host_id already on record, or a pool_id already held by another master host, is 409: only a token bound to a revoked host may re-issue that host, and it must present that host and its pool (409 otherwise). A separate authenticated Core-local peer flow can subsequently join a member; this enrollment endpoint neither joins members nor changes master. The same key is the same host: a request whose CSR matches a recorded active credential (a retry after a lost response, even with a new token) returns that credential unchanged. Issues a 90-day host-specific client certificate and CA. The token binds to its first CSR; an identical token/CSR retry before token expiry returns the same identity without duplicate enrollment. A different CSR returns 409. After expiry or revocation obtain a new site-bound token; replacement requires explicit revoked host selection. Enrollment has no VM side effects. Compatibility: an older Controller rejects the new fields with 400 (unknown field); upgrade Controller and Core together.

POST /api/v1/agent/report

Report observations and reconcile commands

Implemented in development product 0.1.0. Outbound mutual TLS authenticates exactly one enrolled, unrevoked host. Versions 1 and 2 are accepted; version 2 starts repository negotiation without storage-repositories-v1, waits for the Controller storage_repositories acknowledgement, persists it, then advertises that capability. Clustered storage has its own v2 acknowledgement: a Core sends neither clustered results nor storage-clustered-iscsi-v2 until it receives storage_clusters_support with that exact capability. The Controller sends that acknowledgement on every v2 preflight. A newly reconnected Core may offer the session-monitor preflight while withholding storage-clustered-iscsi-v2; before its acknowledged follow-up report, Controller clustered routes return retryable 503 negotiation pending without dispatching work or falling back. Core resets this readiness on start, Controller replacement/enrollment and report disconnect, so an older strict Controller sees only the clean preflight; queued Core results remain durable until a matching Controller acknowledges. Persist a strictly increasing sequence across restarts; discard superseded reports. Null/omitted inventory is heartbeat only and never makes old checks healthy. Results refer only to this host operations; acknowledge persisted results before deleting local journal entries. Commands can redeliver and must be reconciled by operation_id. Controller reconnect requires fresh inventory; no automatic VM restart is permitted. Sequence range is 1 through 9223372036854775807. Superseded sequences receive 200 but do not update last-seen or inventory; operation results and command redelivery still reconcile. At most 100 results per report; result error is at most 4096 UTF-8 bytes. Results for queued, undelivered operations return 409; known operation IDs belonging to another host return 400. Valid results for unknown operation IDs from a former Controller are acknowledged without creating operations or resource state. Terminal results are acknowledged without rewriting the original outcome, except an authoritative succeeded result for the same host and operation may settle a prior needs_attention outcome after Core recovery. At most 100 pending commands return, in creation order. Inventory fields merge only when inventory observed_at increases; individual checks merge only when their observed_at increases. Controller derives per-check freshness independently from heartbeat freshness. Health changes are recorded as debounced audit transitions (default debounce five seconds, configurable). Reports advertise at most 32 capabilities of up to 100 UTF-8 bytes each. managed-vm-v1 gates new commands; omission prevents managed delivery and a newer sequence clears stored capabilities. Result states include needs_attention for uncertain host effects. Automatic two-host BMC promotion reports the optional automatic=true flag in managed.transfer and managed.promotion; older Core versions omit it, and clients treat omission as false. A later authenticated terminal backup Result from the same host and operation ID can settle an earlier needs_attention Controller operation; backup inventory alone cannot, and cross-host Results remain rejected. After a Result is acknowledged, Core continues reporting the Controller-owned backup Journal outcome; a same-ID native vm-create cannot replace it, and peer-dispatched member work is excluded. Controller updates only its own matching nonterminal host/kind/operation row from this explicit outcome. Recurring backup metadata outcomes use the same rule; Controller adoption binds own operation and resource rows to the reporting host and kind before updating a nonterminal task, so colliding IDs from other hosts or kinds are mirrored separately.

POST /api/v1/agent/rotate

Rotate a host certificate

Implemented in development product 0.1.0, protocol v1. Outbound mutual TLS requires the current valid, unrevoked host certificate. CSR binds the next certificate to the same host. Persist identity atomically; retain recovery access on an ambiguous response. No VM side effects. Requires signed PEM ECDSA P-256 CSR. The new certificate lasts 90 days; previous certificates overlap for at most ten minutes. Repeating the same CSR while authenticated returns the existing unexpired certificate. After the overlap expires, use persisted new identity or explicitly revoke and re-enroll.

POST /api/v1/appliances/bootstrap

Create initial appliance site and enrollment intent

Administrator-only appliance bootstrap. Persist a stable request_id and random 64-character lowercase hexadecimal enrollment_token before submission. The same request, names and token return the original site without duplicates. Payload changes conflict. An authenticated replay refreshes token expiry to ten minutes without clearing a consumed token's CSR binding; consumed tokens support replay only of the already-enrolled agent CSR through the existing enrollment endpoint. No pool is created here: the appliance host becomes the master of an automatic pool when it enrolls. This does not create or start a VM. Core enrollment remains outbound verified HTTPS protocol v1. Revoked enrollment tokens are not recreated; use explicit recovery.

POST /api/v1/appliances/adopt

Adopt the existing Controller VM

Register the existing libvirt UUID with a separate host assignment and protected Controller role. The pool is derived from the host record; an optional pool_id must match it (409 otherwise) and the response always returns pool_id. Requires an active host and fresh successful libvirt inventory observing this VM. A UUID reported by another host is rejected, including revoked hosts and old observations: reconcile ownership first. Stable request_id and identical payload replay the original registration; altered payload or owner conflicts. Registration grants no fencing, power, deletion or migration permission.

POST /api/v1/vms

Create a stopped guest VM

Administrator session required. Mutations require same HTTPS Origin and X-CSRF-Token; JSON rejects unknown fields and bodies over 1 MiB. Persist request_id before sending. Identical payload replays return the same resource/operation; changed payload conflicts. New work requires a fresh active host in the selected pool advertising managed-vm-v1. Poll resource lists and operations for terminal results. HTTP acceptance is not host completion. Shared bounds, enforced identically on Controller and Core: 1–8 disks of 1–2048 GiB on virtio, sata or scsi with names unique in the VM; at most 8 NICs on virtio or e1000e with unicast lower-case manual MACs; at least 1 vCPU with sockets × cores × threads equal to the count when a topology is given; at least 512 MiB in memory mode dedicated or maximum; uefi or bios; boot orders unique and positive across disks and install media (gaps are allowed, since ejecting media leaves one), with at least one boot device. Controller additionally caps CPU at 64 and memory at 262144 MiB, assigns the UUID and refuses capacity above the host's observed CPU or memory. The host decides everything its own record answers: VM name and MAC uniqueness against its managed journal and libvirt domains, and dedicated-memory admission against total host memory, are reported as a failed vm-create result with the reason (visible in Task history), not as an HTTP refusal. Storage, network and ISO must have succeeded on this host and pool. The install ISO may be on any verified storage on that host; it need not share a repository with the VM disks. Core journals effects and reconciles per-disk ownership before replay; needs_attention preserves uncertain resources for manual recovery. start_after_create is honoured by the host inside the same creation: once the definition is verified the creation has succeeded, and Core starts the guest once, recording the outcome in the journal entry's start field so a retry never starts it twice. A failed automatic start keeps the VM as a normal stopped managed VM and is reported as a separate failed vm-power outcome (<operation-id>:start, 'VM created but not started: <reason>') in Task history; start it from the Power controls. autostart is a libvirt property set while the stopped VM is defined. No console, overwrite, automatic cleanup of ambiguous disks or guest installation. Core requires 2 GiB available host RAM reserve and verifies KVM/x86-64 and machine-type libvirt capabilities; uefi requires advertised EFI firmware. Failed/uncertain VM names remain reserved; there is no retry/deletion endpoint. A non-empty drivers_media_id requires the host to report vm-media-drivers-drive-v1 (409 "the selected host agent does not support a driver disc drive; upgrade Nex Core") and a succeeded ISO import on the same host and pool (404 "the driver disc ISO is not registered and verified on the selected host and pool"); both are checked after the replay check. Nonempty cpu.features requires vm-cpu-baseline-v1 after idempotent replay (409 on older Core). Core validates the explicit named CPU definition with native hypervisor-cpu-compare against the actual machine before creation/stopped edits/Core-mediated starts. Existing model-only definitions retain prior semantics; no guest-OS-specific CPU filtering. The 202 body may carry an optional warnings array. It is advisory and nothing else — the request was accepted, the pool master still decides, and every refusal, timeout and status is unchanged — and it names each required pool-shared repository, network or ISO whose access on the selected host this Controller's 30-second-old mirror does not show as current. The Controller deliberately does not veto on its mirror: that would make it a second placement authority and would refuse placements the master would accept. Nonempty tags require vm-tags-v1 on the selected host and its pool master after idempotent replay (409 on older Core).

GET /api/v1/storage

List local storage registrations

Administrator inventory of pool registrations with explicit host access and durable operation statuses; read-only and safe to retry. Includes the automatically created default ISO storage (/var/lib/libvirt/images) and storage adopted from Inventory.managed, distinguishable by actor system on their operation. A typed registration the host refused carries id set to this Controller's own request-row key, pending-storage-<operation_id>, which is the handle DELETE /api/v1/storage/{id} takes to discard the failed request record. A registration still queued or dispatched answers id "": Core allocates repository IDs and this Controller never mints one, and on success the row keeps Core's allocated ID.

POST /api/v1/storage/discover

Discover a storage source from Nex Core

Administrator session, same HTTPS Origin and X-CSRF-Token required. The Controller validates pool/host scope then relays one bounded discovery request only to the addressed authenticated Core advertising storage-repositories-v1 and storage-discovery-v1. Discovery is an observation, never a registration: it cannot create directories, mount or log in a source, retain iSCSI nodes/sessions, change repository state or journal work. The Controller keeps the request (including SMB/CHAP credentials when supplied) only in an in-memory request/response relay, deletes it on Core delivery, result, browser cancellation or the 30-second deadline, and writes neither credentials nor candidates to SQLite, a journal, audit log or cache. Core limits work to eight seconds and returns sanitized candidates only; no credentials, device paths, mount options or command output. A 200 result may be empty, failed or stale; 504 is stale when no Core result arrives before the deadline. Retry with a new request ID after timeout or cancellation.

POST /api/v1/storage/zfs/provision

Provision ZFS storage from selected devices

Administrator session, same HTTPS Origin and X-CSRF-Token required. The Controller persists a stable request_id and relays one durable storage-zfs-provision command only to the selected pool master advertising storage-zfs-provision-v1. Every selected host must also be fresh, active, in the selected pool and advertise storage-zfs-provision-v1; otherwise the request is refused with 409 before Core is asked. Core owns the repository identity, validates each selected device immediately before destructive work, executes any selected member work through its authenticated peer channel, journals recovery, and reports the resulting Core-owned repository projection. An accepted request is not proof that devices were changed; poll operations and refreshed host inventory. Identical retries return the original request and operation; a changed payload conflicts.

POST /api/v1/storage/zfs/replace

Replace a failed disk of a provisioned ZFS repository

Administrator session, same HTTPS Origin and X-CSRF-Token required. The Controller persists a stable request_id and relays one durable storage-zfs-replace command to the pool master, which checks that the repository and the host are its own and either runs the work itself or forwards it to that ready current member over the authenticated peer channel. The executing host revalidates the pool and the disk against a fresh observation, then clears the replacement with wipefs --all and runs zpool replace; the operation is done when zpool replace returns. The resilver that follows is ZFS's own work and is read from the repository's ordinary pool observation, and ZFS retires the old disk itself when it finishes. VMs on the pool keep running throughout and nothing waits on the Controller. The refusals below are only what the Controller can already see from its own rows; Core checks the pool, the failed leaf, the replacement and the erase confirmation again, and its own refusals arrive as the operation's result rather than as an HTTP status here. Implemented in development product 0.4.4.

GET /api/v1/storage/cluster

Read Core-owned clustered iSCSI status

Administrator session required. pool_id selects its current active master, which must have acknowledged and advertise storage-clustered-iscsi-v2. During a new Core's bounded v2 preflight, 503 means negotiation is pending: no status relay was sent, so retry after the acknowledged follow-up report. A Core that never offers clustered support remains 409. The Controller forwards one transient status request only after acknowledgement and retains no cluster configuration, job or secret. A 200 is the Core's current durable operation projection; a 504 means the Core did not answer within 30 seconds and is ambiguous, so retry this GET rather than assuming setup stopped. The Controller HTTPS write deadline is 45 seconds only to leave delivery margin for this existing 30-second relay contract; it does not extend Core work.

POST /api/v1/storage/cluster/verify-fence

Ask Core to verify one cluster fence

Administrator session, same HTTPS Origin and X-CSRF-Token required. request_id identifies the destructive attempt; host_id is the target, and fence_confirmation must be exactly FENCE <host_id>. The Controller validates target capability and relays the confirmation transiently to the pool master. It creates no durable fence intent. An immediate accepted response is not a proof: Core records its durable cluster operation as verifying_fence with a request-bound unverified pending proof, and performs the actual exclusion observation only at the executor. Browser input cannot claim a proof. An early failed observation is uncertain. The unchanged relay deadline is 30 seconds; the Controller's 45-second HTTPS write deadline only leaves response-delivery margin. A timeout is ambiguous: the UI closes the dialog and disables that target until a successful Core status refresh, without automatic retry. A refreshed failed or uncertain proof may be manually reverified only with a new request_id and a new exact confirmation; Core retains the prior proof. A pending unverified proof remains disabled. This is existing recovery behavior, not a new interface.
